why: How every Temporal client in this repository is told to use TLS. The contract is ENVIRONMENT, and it is shared by three languages and sixteen client connections: the orchestrator (TypeScript), the handler and the Go host, both Python hosts, and six CLI commands. Before this, none of them could connect to a secured Temporal at all — every site spelled `connect({address})` and stopped — so a self-hoster who put Temporal behind mTLS, the ordinary thing to do with a server holding every Run's history, had no way to point kontra at it.
why_a_corpus: Sixteen sites is the whole difficulty. A change reaching twelve of them does not fail loudly: it produces a deployment that mostly works and has one process talking plaintext to a server that accepts both — the worst of the three outcomes, because it looks like the good one. Three independent implementations of one env contract is exactly the shape ADR 0035 rule two says gets a corpus rather than three tables of literals.
the_two_invariants: PLAINTEXT IS THE DEFAULT. With none of these set, every implementation must produce exactly what it produced before this existed. An existing deployment cannot be broken by the feature arriving.

ANY ONE SETTING TURNS TLS ON. Setting a CA and forgetting the switch would otherwise read the certificate, build nothing from it, and connect in the clear — a silent downgrade produced by configuration that looks complete.
refusals: A misconfiguration is a REFUSAL and never a fall back to plaintext: an unreadable file, or a client certificate without its key. A security setting that degrades to off when it cannot be satisfied is the failure `watchdog.sh` shipped for years in this repository and the shape ADR 0039 refuses for cosign. The error names the VARIABLE and the PATH — an operator needs to know which setting pointed where, and a path is a filesystem location. It never contains key material or a passphrase.

cases.why: nothing set: plaintext, and byte-identical to what every call site passed before
the switch alone: TLS with the system trust store, no private CA, no client pair
THE SILENT DOWNGRADE THIS CLOSES: a CA with no switch must still turn TLS on
a client pair with no switch turns TLS on too, for the same reason
an SNI override alone turns TLS on — it is meaningless without it
the full mTLS shape: private CA, client pair and an SNI override for a proxy in front
the switch explicitly off, with nothing else set, is plaintext
OFF DOES NOT OVERRIDE A CA. The switch turns TLS ON; it is not a master disable, and a reading where it silently discards a configured certificate is the downgrade again

refusal_cases.why: a certificate without its key cannot authenticate; the server would refuse the handshake without naming either variable
an unreadable CA is a refusal, naming the variable and the path — never plaintext

notes: `@ca`, `@crt` and `@key` are placeholders: a driver writes temporary PEM files and substitutes the paths. They must be a REAL, self-signed pair rather than arbitrary bytes — the Go implementation calls tls.X509KeyPair at configuration time so that an unusable pair is refused there rather than surfacing later as a handshake failure that names nothing. Generating one per run is a few lines in each language and is why the corpus carries no key material: a fixture holding a private key is a fixture nobody should commit, even a throwaway one.

The implementations differ in HOW MUCH they validate and that is deliberate, not drift. Go parses the pair and the CA pool because crypto/tls gives it those checks for free; TypeScript hands the bytes to the Temporal SDK, which validates at connect. What the corpus pins is the DECISION — TLS on or off, which material is present, and which misconfigurations are refusals — because that is the part an operator configures and the part that must not disagree across sixteen client connections.
